claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation during sustained loading of HEA multilayers is driven by interface-induced elastic undulations.
Elastic undulations lower the local activation barrier for dislocation nucleation.
Elastic undulations promote cooperative dislocation slip.
Inherent lattice distortion intensifies interface elastic undulations.
Spatial variations in short-range order intensify interface elastic undulations.
The mismatch in mechanical response between FCC and BCC layers under sustained loading produces localized elastic undulations at their interfaces.
The relevant stripelike elastic undulations have a characteristic wavelength of approximately 1–2 nm.
The proposed coating consists of alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC HEA layers with sharp interfaces.
Greater short-range order will produce a faster creep rate than lower short-range order under otherwise comparable conditions.
More pronounced interface-induced elastic undulations will produce a faster creep rate.
Higher-SRO coatings will develop higher interfacial dislocation and twin densities than lower-SRO coatings.
Regions exhibiting 1–2 nm interface undulations will correlate with increased localized plastic deformation.
Homogenization annealing temperature can be used to vary chemical short-range order.
At sufficiently high temperatures, thermal diffusion may dominate deformation instead of the proposed interface-mediated mechanism.
At high strain rates, deformation mechanisms other than interface-mediated undulation, slip, and twinning may dominate.
The starting baseline is defined as having no elastic-undulation features and minimal preexisting dislocations.
A lack of significant differences in undulations, dislocation or twin nucleation, and creep rate between high-SRO and low-SRO samples would falsify the hypothesis.
